covers.quote: If your organisation uses the documentary–note system, change the citation and reference list styles accordingly.
Use the author–date system for in-text citations in documents with a reference list.
Use the author–date system for in-text citations in documents with a reference list.

rules.quote: Cite plays and poetry using the author–date system.
rules.violation_condition: A citation to a play or poem uses a system other than author–date, although the organisation has not adopted the documentary–note system.
when: If the organisation uses the documentary–note system, its citation and reference list styles apply instead.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the organisational exception with the rule; G-4 consolidates its repeated statements.

rules.quote: You must attribute copyright material you reference.
rules.violation_condition: Referenced copyright material from a play, poem or script has no attribution.
when: The referenced material is protected by copyright.
This includes plays, poems and scripts.
rules.why: This is an explicit attribution requirement, distinct from the detailed citation formats.

rules.quote: Include all the details required by open access licences (read how to attribute Creative Commons).
rules.violation_condition: An attribution for material used under an open access licence omits a detail required by that licence.
when: The material is used under an open access licence.
Determine the required details from the applicable licence.
rules.why: The licence-specific completeness check is distinct from merely having an attribution.

covers.quote: Write titles of plays in italics and use sentence case.
Use italics for the title of the play.

rules.quote: Use italics and sentence case for titles of plays
rules.violation_condition: A play title is not italicised or is capitalised other than in sentence case.
when: Sentence case gives an initial capital to the first word and proper nouns.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the body restatement and the repeated instruction for reviews into one play-title styling check.

covers.quote: When you quote lines spoken by a character in a play, use a forward slash to show line breaks appearing in the original. Insert spaces around the forward slash. If there's a line break in your text, it can occur before or after the slash.
Use a forward slash to show line breaks in poems
Separate lines of poetry in a sentence with a forward slash. Insert spaces around the forward slash. If there's a line break in your text, it can occur before or after the slash.

rules.quote: Use a forward slash to show line breaks in plays
rules.violation_condition: A quotation running across original verse lines does not mark the line boundaries with forward slashes, or its line-break slashes lack surrounding spaces.
when: For plays, the quotation contains lines spoken by a character.
For poems, lines of poetry are presented within a sentence.
A line break in the new text may occur before or after the slash.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4 consolidate the same spaced-slash convention for play dialogue and poetry, including its wrapping permission.

covers.quote: In plays, you don’t need quotation marks if the direct speech follows the name of the speaker.

rules.quote: Don’t use quotation marks in scripts of plays
rules.violation_condition: Direct speech in a play script is enclosed in quotation marks even though it follows the speaker’s name.
when: The direct speech follows the name of the speaker.
rules.why: The heading supplies the recommendation; G-2 uses the body to limit it to speech following a speaker’s name.

covers.quote: Citations to plays are more helpful if you use divisions – acts, scenes and lines.
Use divisions if they are available

rules.quote: Use divisions for in-text citations of plays
rules.violation_condition: A citation locating a passage in a play, or in a poem with numbered divisions, omits the relevant divisions.
when: Play divisions include acts, scenes and lines.
For poems, use divisions when they are marked and numbered in the text.
Poem divisions can include cantos, verses, stanzas and lines.
Ancient and medieval dramatic works have separate citation rules under classics.
rules.why: G-2 combines the same passage-locator check, with availability limiting its application to poems.

covers.quote: Use the poet’s full name, unless people can identify the poet by the surname alone.

rules.quote: Use the full name of the playwright, unless people can identify the playwright by the surname.
rules.specification: The page gives no recognisability threshold or list of authors identifiable by surname. Applying the exception requires a judgement about the intended readership.
rules.violation_condition: A citation uses only a playwright’s or poet’s surname when that surname does not identify the person adequately for the intended readers.
when: A surname alone is sufficient when readers can identify the playwright or poet by it.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4 consolidate the identical full-name requirement and its audience-dependent exception.

covers.quote: Use lower case and numerals for divisions.
For subsequent citations, you can use just use the division numbers, without the words ‘part’, ‘verse’ or ‘lines’.

rules.quote: Use roman type (not italics), lower case and numerals for divisions.
rules.violation_condition: A division locator uses capitalised division labels or spelled-out numbers, or a play’s division locator is italicised.
when: Lower-case division labels and numerals apply to plays and poems.
The explicit roman-type requirement is stated for plays.
Subsequent poem citations may omit the words ‘part’, ‘verse’ and ‘lines’ and use division numbers alone.
The separately specified ‘Sonnet X’ form for Shakespeare’s sonnets is not a lower-case division label.
rules.why: G-2 combines division-notation cases and retains the subsequent-citation permission as an exception.

covers.quote: In government content, you don’t need to create a reference list just to cite plays. If you have a reference list already, then add plays to your list. You can also add reviews of plays to the list.
Include poems if you’re using a reference list
You don’t need to create a separate reference list to cite poems, but if you have a reference list already, then add poems to your list.

rules.quote: Include plays if you’re using a reference list
rules.violation_condition: A document has a reference list but omits a play or poem cited in the document.
when: There is already a reference list.
A reference list need not be created solely to cite plays or poems.
Reviews of plays may also be included.
rules.why: G-2 to G-4 consolidate the repeated reference-list requirement and retain permissions without creating additional rules.

covers.quote: Use the edition of the poem you cited.

rules.quote: Use the edition of the play you cited.
rules.violation_condition: A reference list entry identifies a different edition from the edition of the play or poem actually cited.
when: A play or poem is included in a reference list.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the identical edition-matching requirement for plays and poems.

covers.quote: If the poem was written well before the edition, place the original date in parentheses with the edition’s publishing date.
Use the original and edition dates if citing an old work.
Use the original and edition dates if citing an old work.

rules.quote: If the play was written well before the edition, place the original date in parentheses with the edition’s publishing date.
rules.specification: The page does not define ‘well before’ or ‘old work’. A reviewer must resolve which works qualify. The supplied author–date templates show the original year and edition year separated by a slash; reference-entry years are enclosed together in parentheses.
rules.violation_condition: A reference entry or in-text citation for an old play or poem gives the edition date without the original date.
when: The work was written well before the cited edition, described elsewhere on the page as an old work.
Apply the two-date requirement to both reference entries and in-text citations.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4 consolidate the old-work date requirement across both literary forms and both citation locations.

rules.quote: Rule: Author A (Year of Original Publication/Year of Edition) Title of play: subtitle of play, Name of Publisher of Edition, Place of Publication.
rules.violation_condition: An author–date reference list entry for a play omits a required bibliographic field or arranges and punctuates its fields contrary to the supplied play-reference template.
when: The entry is for a published edition of a play in an author–date reference list.
The sequence is author surname and initials, parenthesised year information, title and any subtitle, edition publisher, and place of publication.
The separate old-work date rule determines whether both original and edition years are needed.
The separate play-title rule governs italics and capitalisation.
rules.why: The explicit template supplies one reference-entry structure check; separate rules handle edition accuracy, conditional dates and title styling.

covers.quote: Include a page number after a colon if you’re citing a specific page.

rules.quote: Include a page number after a colon if you’re citing a specific page.
rules.violation_condition: An author–date citation to a specific page of a play or poem omits the page number or does not place it after a colon following the year.
when: The document has a reference list and uses author–date in-text citations.
The citation is to a specific page.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the verbatim repeated page-locator requirement.
